faq.q: How do I stop racing thoughts at night?
faq.a: Write a specific to-do list for five minutes before bed, handle real worries earlier in the evening by writing a next step for each, and if you're still awake after about 15 to 20 minutes, get up and do something quiet until you feel sleepy. Trying to suppress the thoughts tends to make it take longer to fall asleep.

faq.q: Does writing a to-do list before bed help you sleep?
faq.a: In a 2018 Baylor sleep-lab study of 57 young adults, people who spent five minutes writing a to-do list fell asleep about nine minutes faster than people who wrote about tasks they had finished. The more specific the list, the faster they fell asleep. It was a single night with people who didn't have insomnia, so treat it as promising rather than proven.

faq.q: Why do my thoughts race when I try to sleep?
faq.a: Lying in the dark is often the first moment all day when nothing demands your attention, so unfinished tasks, unsolved problems and unprocessed feelings come back. Research on people with insomnia finds their pre-sleep thoughts are often about planning or problem-solving, and that worry raises arousal, which makes sleep harder.

faq.q: Do breathing exercises help with racing thoughts at night?
faq.a: They can help some people. A small 2015 study found that 20 minutes of slow breathing at about six breaths a minute before bed shortened the time it took people with insomnia to fall asleep. The evidence is still limited, so treat breathing as one useful tool, not a cure.

faq.q: When should I see a doctor about racing thoughts at night?
faq.a: If racing thoughts keep you awake most nights for weeks, or poor sleep makes daily life hard, talk to a doctor. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the recommended first treatment for chronic insomnia, and a clinician can check for anxiety, depression or other sleep disorders.

informationGain: Instead of a generic tip list, it sorts bedtime thoughts into three kinds (tasks, unsolved problems, unprocessed feelings) and matches each to the specific technique trials have tested for it, with each study's size and limits, plus evidence that suppression backfires and that sleep hygiene alone isn't recommended.
